segments.text: We use AI by having a conversation. You ask a question in plain English, like,
what's the best Avengers movie? And the AI replies with a detailed answer,
just like a person would. But behind that screen, AI doesn't understand English.
It runs on math. It only processes numbers. So how does the system translate your written
words into a mathematical language it can calculate? The most obvious approach would
be to assign a unique number to every single word in the dictionary. But that system breaks
down almost immediately. People constantly invent new slang, make typos, and type in code or emojis.
A list of a million words still wouldn't cover everything a person might type into a chat box.
Instead of trying to memorize every possible whole word, AI uses reusable text pieces called tokens.
Think of them as the basic building blocks for language. A token can be a whole word,
or it can be just a small fragment of one. Take a multi-syllable word like unbelievable.
The AI doesn't view this as a single unit. It splits the word into three distinct chunks,
un, belie, and vable. This system is incredibly efficient because those fragments are reusable.
That exact same un prefix can be combined with other pieces to build unusual or unmatchable.
The AI's vocabulary doesn't need a brand new entry for every single variation of a word.
By shattering language into these universal pieces, AI creates a flexible, finite system.
It only needs to track a set number of blocks to process an infinite variety of human sentences.
Before you ever open a chat window, engineers use programs to analyze massive collections of text.
This analysis determines exactly how words will be split and establishes the AI's permanent
vocabulary list. These vocabularies are large, but highly optimized. ChatGPT holds about 200,000
distinct tokens, while Google's Gemini uses about 256,000 to cover human communication.
Every single token on that list gets assigned its own specific number, called a token ID.
It acts like an exact address in the AI's vocabulary catalog.
So when you type a message and hit send, a program called a tokenizer steps in. It breaks your text
down into those reusable chunks, and then looks up the numerical ID for each one. Unbelievable
instantly becomes the numbers 359, 32898, and 24694. But we have to make a strict distinction here.
The tokenizer converts the written word cat into ID number 4719. That number only identifies the
specific text fragment. To the AI at this precise step in the process, 4719 tells it absolutely
nothing about what a cat actually is. It is just a catalog number, not a mathematical representation
of fur, whiskers, or a small animal. Tokenization is strictly the entry point. It provides the
translation so that the actual meaning of those words can be calculated by the model's neural
network later on. This chart shows how a tokenizer handles everything. ChatGPT is
chopped into three tokens, chat, g, and pt. In iHeartAI, spaces aren't ignored,
they are actively bundled into the tokens themselves, totaling three distinct chunks.
Finally, a standard web address is methodically sliced into eight smaller bits.
Every single letter, space, and symbol you enter into the prompt is mathematically accounted for.
It is converted into a numeric unit before the AI ever begins to formulate a response.
When the AI has calculated its answer, the journey happens in reverse. The model outputs a sequence
of token IDs, and the tokenizer converts those numbers back into their corresponding text
fragments. Those fragments are then stitched tightly together, creating the final coherent
sentences that appear on your screen. Words become numbers. That lets AI work with your
language using math.
